meta.title: London landscape history: walls and defences, parks and squares, terrain relief blobs, and pre-urban forest and marsh cover
meta.coordinate_system: WGS84 lon,lat decimal degrees, 5 decimal places
meta.terrain_model: Each terrain entry is a Gaussian blob for procedural relief: elevation contribution = height_m * exp(-((d/sigma_m)^2)/2) where d is horizontal distance in metres from (lon,lat). height_m is the RELIEF above the surrounding plain, not absolute altitude; elevation_m_aod gives the real summit height above Ordnance Datum for reference. A London Clay/Thames-terrace base plane of about 5-15 m AOD is assumed. Summing overlapping blobs will over-shoot; consider a max() or soft-max blend for adjacent ridge entries.
meta.accuracy_note: Polygons and polylines are hand-authored generalisations digitised by eye. Wall and Civil War alignments are archaeological/antiquarian reconstructions. Land-cover polygons for c.1 CE are schematic envelopes based on geology and place-name evidence, not mapped boundaries. Items with weak evidence are flagged (?).

walls.name: London Wall (landward circuit)
walls.material: Kentish ragstone with tile bonding courses, earth bank behind
walls.notes: Built c.AD 190-225 (dendrochronology and coin evidence from the Blackfriars and Tower sections narrow it to about AD 200), enclosing roughly 130 ha - the largest civil engineering project in Roman Britain. Around 85,000 tonnes of Kentish ragstone were barged up the Thames; a ragstone barge that sank c.AD 63 was found at Blackfriars in 1962. Incorporated the north and west walls of the earlier Cripplegate fort (c.AD 120). External bastions were added c.AD 350. The wall determined the shape of the City for 1500 years; the medieval wall was largely the Roman wall repaired and heightened. Demolition of the gates 1760-1767; substantial fragments survive at Tower Hill, Cooper's Row, Noble Street and St Alphage.

walls.name: London Wall (riverside wall)
walls.notes: A later riverside wall closing the south side of the circuit, dated by dendrochronology to c.AD 255-270 (with a rebuild c.AD 390 at the Tower). Built partly of reused monumental stone, including sculptures from a demolished temple and a monumental arch found at Blackfriars in 1975. Decayed and was robbed out in the Saxon and early medieval periods as the waterfront advanced south over it.

walls.name: Cripplegate Roman fort
walls.notes: A 4.5 ha auxiliary/garrison fort built c.AD 120 in the north-west corner of Londinium, discovered from bomb-site excavation in 1949-1956. Its west and north walls were thickened and incorporated into the city wall c.AD 200, which is why the wall has a distinct rectangular bulge there. The double west gate survives in a car park under London Wall.

walls.name: City gates

gates.name: Ludgate
gates.notes: Roman origin; rebuilt 1215 and 1586, used as a debtors' prison from 1378. Demolished 1760.

gates.name: Newgate
gates.notes: Roman origin; a prison from 1188 until Newgate Prison closed in 1902. Gate demolished 1767.

gates.name: Aldersgate
gates.notes: A late-Roman insertion (c.AD 350), not part of the original circuit. Rebuilt 1617. Demolished 1761.

gates.name: Cripplegate
gates.notes: Originally the north gate of the Cripplegate fort (c.AD 120), later a city gate. Demolished 1760.

gates.name: Moorgate
gates.notes: Not Roman: a postern of 1415, widened into a full gate, giving access to the marshy Moorfields. Demolished 1762.

gates.name: Bishopsgate
gates.notes: The gate for Ermine Street and the Great North Road. Demolished 1760.

gates.name: Aldgate
gates.notes: The gate for the Colchester road. Geoffrey Chaucer leased the rooms above it 1374-1386. Demolished 1761.

gates.name: Tower Postern
gates.notes: A postern at the south-east angle, collapsed 1440 (?).

gates.name: Bridge Gate
gates.notes: The Southwark end of Old London Bridge, where traitors' heads were displayed on pikes from 1305 (William Wallace) until 1678.

gates.name: Billingsgate / Dowgate water gates
gates.notes: Riverside water-gates and docks rather than land gates; dates approximate (?).

walls.notes: Seven principal land gates (Ludgate, Newgate, Aldersgate, Cripplegate, Moorgate, Bishopsgate, Aldgate). All were demolished between 1760 and 1767 by the City Corporation to ease traffic; their names survive as street and ward names.

walls.name: Temple Bar
walls.notes: The ceremonial western boundary of the City on Fleet Street, first recorded as a chain and posts in 1293 and a timber gatehouse by the 14th century. Wren's Portland stone arch of 1670-1672 replaced the structure that survived the Great Fire. Removed in 1878 because it obstructed traffic, re-erected at Theobalds Park in Hertfordshire in 1880, and returned to the City at Paternoster Square in 2004. The Temple Bar Memorial griffin of 1880 marks the original site. The Lord Mayor still meets the monarch here by tradition.

walls.name: Lines of Communication (English Civil War defences)

forts.name: Mount Mill fort, St John Street
Black Mary's Hole fort, Bagnigge Wells

walls.notes: An earthwork ring of ramparts and ditches with 23 forts and redoubts, thrown up by Parliament in 1642-1643 at 1.5 to 2 miles from the City to protect London from the Royalist army after Edgehill and Brentford. About 20,000 Londoners - men, women and children, organised by trained bands and livery companies - built the works in under two months in the spring of 1643. Never attacked. Demolished by order of Parliament in 1647 after the New Model Army occupied London. Almost nothing survives above ground; the circuit is reconstructed from Vertue's 1738 map after a lost contemporary plan, so individual fort positions are approximate (?).

parks.name: Hyde Park
parks.notes: Seized by Henry VIII from Westminster Abbey in 1536 as a deer park; opened to the public by Charles I in 1637. The Serpentine 1730; the Great Exhibition's Crystal Palace stood here 1851-1852; Speakers' Corner from 1872.

parks.name: St James's Park
parks.notes: Marshy ground by the Tyburn acquired by Henry VIII in 1532; drained and laid out formally for Charles II from 1660 and opened to the public; remodelled in naturalistic style by John Nash 1827-1828. The oldest of the royal parks.

parks.name: Green Park
parks.notes: Enclosed as Upper St James's Park by Charles II in 1668, reputedly on a burial ground for lepers, which is why it has almost no flowerbeds. Site of Handel's Music for the Royal Fireworks, 1749.

parks.name: Kensington Gardens
parks.notes: Carved out of Hyde Park for Queen Caroline 1728-1730 by Charles Bridgeman, with the Round Pond, the Broad Walk and the Long Water. Opened to respectably dressed public on Saturdays from 1728 and fully in 1841. Albert Memorial 1872; Peter Pan statue 1912.

parks.name: Regent's Park
parks.notes: Formerly Marylebone Park, a Tudor hunting ground leased as farmland until the Crown lease fell in in 1811. John Nash's masterplan of 1811 laid out the terraces, the Inner and Outer Circles and the lake; opened to the public in 1835 (two days a week) and fully by 1841. London Zoo 1828; Queen Mary's Gardens 1932.

parks.name: Greenwich Park
parks.notes: The oldest enclosed royal park: Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester walled 200 acres in 1433. Replanted to a formal plan attributed to Andre Le Notre for Charles II in the 1660s. Royal Observatory 1675, the Prime Meridian. Contains Anglo-Saxon barrows and a Roman temple site.

parks.name: Richmond Park
parks.notes: Walled by Charles I in 1637 as a deer park during a plague year, to the fury of local commoners. Public right of way established by John Lewis's lawsuit in 1758. The largest of the royal parks and a National Nature Reserve; still holds about 600 red and fallow deer. King Henry's Mound has a protected sightline to St Paul's, 16 km away.

parks.name: Bushy Park
parks.notes: Taken with Hampton Court by Henry VIII in 1529 and enclosed as a deer park. The Chestnut Avenue and Diana Fountain laid out by Wren for William III, 1699. SHAEF headquarters for the D-Day planning, 1942-1944.

parks.name: Hampton Court Home Park
parks.notes: The Long Water canal cut for Charles II in 1662.

parks.name: Victoria Park
parks.notes: The first purpose-built public park in Britain, created after an 1840 petition of 30,000 East End signatures to Queen Victoria citing the district's death rate. Land bought 1842, laid out by James Pennethorne, opened 1845. 'The People's Park'; a centre of Chartist, radical and trade-union meetings.

parks.name: Battersea Park
parks.notes: Created out of Battersea Fields under an Act of 1846, the ground raised about 1.5 m with spoil from the Surrey Commercial Docks; opened 1858. Festival Pleasure Gardens 1951; Peace Pagoda 1985.

parks.name: Finsbury Park
parks.notes: Opened 7 August 1869 on Hornsey Wood House land, the first park created by the Metropolitan Board of Works; named for the Finsbury district it was meant to serve, 5 km away.

parks.name: Southwark Park
parks.notes: Opened 19 June 1869, one of the first two MBW parks (with Finsbury Park), on former market gardens in Rotherhithe.

parks.name: Kennington Park
parks.notes: Kennington Common, a site of public executions until 1800 and of the great Chartist meeting of 10 April 1848, was enclosed and laid out as a park in 1852-1854 - partly to prevent further mass meetings. Prince Albert's Model Dwellings of 1851 were re-erected here from the Great Exhibition.

parks.name: Clapham Common
parks.notes: Ancient manorial waste, drained and planted from 1720s; the Clapham Sect of abolitionists lived round it from the 1790s. Vested in the Metropolitan Board of Works in 1877-78, which preserved it from enclosure.

parks.name: Hampstead Heath
parks.notes: Manorial waste of the manor of Hampstead. Sir Thomas Maryon Wilson tried repeatedly from 1829 to 1870 to enclose and build on it; after his death the Metropolitan Board of Works bought the commoners' rights under the Hampstead Heath Act 1871, one of the founding victories of the open-space movement. Extended by Parliament Hill Fields (1889), Golders Hill (1898) and the Kenwood estate (1922-1928).

parks.name: Wimbledon Common and Putney Heath
parks.notes: Earl Spencer's attempt to enclose the common was defeated by the Wimbledon and Putney Commons Act 1871, which vested it in conservators elected by local ratepayers - the first such body in England. Includes Caesar's Camp, an Iron Age hillfort.

parks.name: Blackheath
parks.notes: Manorial waste on the Blackheath plateau; muster point for Wat Tyler (1381) and Jack Cade (1450), and the site of the first recorded game of golf in England (1608). Protected as public open space by the MBW from 1871.

parks.name: Hackney Marshes
parks.notes: Lammas land on the Lea floodplain, bought for the public by the LCC in 1893 after a campaign against enclosure. Levelled with Blitz rubble after 1945 and laid out with what were long the most football pitches in Europe (88 at peak).

parks.name: Epping Forest
parks.notes: The surviving fragment of the royal Forest of Waltham/Essex. Between 1851 and 1871 lords of the manor illegally enclosed about 3000 ha; the City of London Corporation, as a commoner through a Little Ilford cemetery, sued and won in 1874. The Epping Forest Act 1878 vested it in the Corporation, and Queen Victoria dedicated it to the public 'for the enjoyment of my people for ever' at Chingford on 6 May 1882. Ancient wood pasture with about 50,000 pollarded hornbeams and beeches.

parks.name: Hainault Forest
parks.notes: The other half of the Forest of Essex. Disafforested by Act in 1851; about 400 ha were grubbed up in six weeks in 1851-52 and ploughed. The remnant was bought for the public by the LCC and Essex CC in 1903-1906 after a campaign by Edward North Buxton.

parks.name: Crystal Palace Park
parks.notes: Laid out by Joseph Paxton for the re-erected Crystal Palace, opened by Queen Victoria on 10 June 1854. Contains Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins's 1854 concrete dinosaurs, the first life-size reconstructions of extinct animals anywhere. The Palace burned down 30 November 1936; the transmitter mast dates from 1956.

parks.name: Alexandra Park
parks.notes: Opened as a public park in 1863; Alexandra Palace, 'the People's Palace', opened 24 May 1873 and burned down 16 days later, reopening in 1875. The BBC transmitted the world's first regular high-definition public television service from here on 2 November 1936. Internment camp 1914-1919.

parks.name: Brockwell Park
parks.notes: The Brockwell Hall estate (house 1811-13) bought by the LCC and opened 6 June 1892 after a campaign by Thomas Lynn Bristowe MP, who collapsed and died on the steps of the hall on opening day. Lido 1937.

parks.name: Dulwich Park
parks.notes: Given by the Dulwich College Estate and opened by Lord Rosebery in 1890; laid out by Charles Barry the younger. Barbara Hepworth's Two Forms (Divided Circle) was stolen from here in 2011.

parks.name: Peckham Rye Common and Park
parks.notes: The common (Peckham Rye) is ancient manorial waste secured for the public in 1868; the adjoining park was added in 1894. William Blake reported seeing 'a tree filled with angels' on the Rye as a boy, c.1765.

parks.name: Gunnersbury Park
parks.notes: The Rothschild estate bought by Ealing and Acton councils and opened by Neville Chamberlain on 21 May 1926.

parks.name: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew
parks.notes: Princess Augusta's nine-acre botanic garden of 1759 within the royal estate; the Pagoda 1762, the Palm House 1848, the Temperate House 1863. Transferred to the state in 1840 under William Hooker. UNESCO World Heritage Site 2003.

parks.name: Bushy and Home Park deer lawns
parks.notes: Grouped with Bushy Park; included as a separate landscape unit if needed (?).

parks.name: Holland Park
parks.notes: The grounds of Holland House (1605); the house was gutted by incendiary bombs in 1940 and the estate bought by the LCC in 1952.

parks.name: Tooting Bec Common
parks.notes: Tooting Bec Lido, 1906, the largest freshwater open-air pool in England.

parks.name: Woolwich Common
parks.notes: Bought by the Board of Ordnance in 1774 for the Royal Artillery; used as a military parade and training ground ever since, which is why it survived unbuilt. Royal Artillery Barracks (1776-1802) has the longest Georgian facade in Britain.

parks.name: Hounslow Heath
parks.notes: Once 1600 ha of heath stretching from Hounslow to Staines, the site of the Ordnance Survey's founding baseline measured by General Roy in 1784, and of James I's and James II's army camps. Enclosed from 1818; the remainder was taken for Hounslow Barracks, gravel pits, Hounslow Heath Aerodrome (1914) and Heathrow Airport (1944). Only about 80 ha of heathland survive as a Local Nature Reserve.

parks.name: Kensal Green Cemetery
parks.notes: The first of the 'Magnificent Seven' private garden cemeteries, consecrated 24 January 1833, founded by the General Cemetery Company after the 1832 cholera epidemic exposed the state of the overcrowded City churchyards. Greek Revival buildings and catacombs; buried here are Brunel, Trollope, Thackeray and Blondin.

parks.name: West Norwood Cemetery
parks.notes: Consecrated 1837; the first cemetery in the Gothic Revival style. Greek Orthodox necropolis; graves of Mrs Beeton, Hiram Maxim, Henry Doulton.

parks.name: Highgate Cemetery
parks.notes: Consecrated 20 May 1839; the Egyptian Avenue and Circle of Lebanon are the most theatrical Victorian funerary architecture in Britain. The East Cemetery opened 1860 and holds Karl Marx (1883, monument 1956) and George Eliot. Abandoned and overgrown by the 1970s; rescued by the Friends of Highgate Cemetery from 1975.

parks.name: Abney Park Cemetery
parks.notes: Opened 1840 as a wholly non-denominational cemetery and arboretum, the burial ground of choice for Nonconformists and dissenters (William and Catherine Booth of the Salvation Army). Planted with 2500 named tree and shrub species in alphabetical order.

parks.name: Brompton Cemetery
parks.notes: Opened 1840, designed by Benjamin Baud as an open-air cathedral with a Great Circle and catacombs. Nationalised in 1852, the only Crown-owned cemetery in Britain, run by The Royal Parks.

parks.name: Nunhead Cemetery
parks.notes: Consecrated 1840; closed and abandoned in 1969, reclaimed by Southwark from 1975. Famous view of St Paul's from the top of the hill.

parks.name: Tower Hamlets Cemetery
parks.notes: Opened 1841; about 350,000 burials, the great majority in public (pauper) graves. Closed 1966 and now Tower Hamlets Cemetery Park, a woodland nature reserve.

parks.name: City of London Cemetery, Manor Park
parks.notes: Opened 24 June 1856 by the City Corporation on Little Ilford manor land, to receive remains cleared from City churchyards closed under the Burial Acts of the 1850s. One of the largest municipal cemeteries in Europe. The Corporation's status as a commoner here gave it the standing to sue over Epping Forest in 1874.

parks.name: Bunhill Fields
parks.notes: A Nonconformist burial ground from 1665, never consecrated; Bunyan, Defoe, Blake and Susanna Wesley are buried here. Closed 1854, laid out as a public garden 1867.

parks.name: Lincoln's Inn Fields
parks.notes: London's largest public square. Laid out from 1638 to a plan attributed to Inigo Jones after a long fight against building on the fields; the site of the execution of Lord William Russell (1683). Bought for the public by the LCC in 1895.

parks.name: Bloomsbury Square
parks.notes: Laid out by the 4th Earl of Southampton c.1661 as 'Southampton Square', the first London space actually called a square and the model for the Georgian estate square.

parks.name: St James's Square
parks.notes: Laid out by the Earl of St Albans from 1665, the grandest aristocratic square of the Restoration.

parks.name: Hanover Square
parks.notes: Laid out 1713-1717 for Whig grandees and named for the new dynasty.

parks.name: Cavendish Square
parks.notes: Begun 1717 for the Earl of Oxford's Marylebone estate; halted by the South Sea Bubble of 1720 and not finished until the 1770s.

parks.name: Grosvenor Square
parks.notes: Laid out 1725-1731 for Sir Richard Grosvenor, 2.4 ha, the largest and grandest of the West End squares. US Embassy 1960-2018.

parks.name: Berkeley Square
parks.notes: Laid out from 1738 on the gardens of Berkeley House; its plane trees, planted 1789, are among the oldest in London.

parks.name: Portman Square
parks.notes: Begun 1764 for Henry William Portman; Home House (Robert Adam, 1773-77) is on the north side.

parks.name: Manchester Square
parks.notes: Hertford House (1776) now holds the Wallace Collection.

parks.name: Bedford Square
parks.notes: Built 1775-1783; the most complete surviving Georgian square in London, with unified palace-fronted terraces.

parks.name: Russell Square
parks.notes: Laid out 1800-1804 by Humphry Repton for the Duke of Bedford on the gardens of the demolished Bedford House; one of the largest squares in London.

parks.name: Fitzroy Square
parks.notes: East and south sides by Robert Adam, 1794-1798; north and west sides not completed until 1827-1835 because of the Napoleonic wars.

parks.name: Sloane Square
parks.notes: Laid out 1771 on the Hans Sloane estate at the junction of the King's Road and the Chelsea approach.

parks.name: Belgrave Square
parks.notes: Thomas Cubitt's centrepiece for the Grosvenor estate's Belgravia, begun 1826 on the raised Five Fields; 4.5 ha, ringed by stuccoed palaces, now largely embassies.

parks.name: Eaton Square
parks.notes: Begun 1827, Cubitt again; the longest square in London, six garden compartments strung along the King's Road.

parks.name: Trafalgar Square
parks.notes: Created by John Nash's Charing Cross Improvement scheme from 1826 on the site of the Great Mews; laid out by Charles Barry and completed 1845. Nelson's Column 1843, the lions 1867, the fountains 1845 (rebuilt 1939).

parks.name: Paternoster Square and Finsbury Circus
parks.notes: Finsbury Circus (1815-1817) was the first public garden in the City, laid out on the drained Moorfields; Paternoster Square is a 1960s and 2003 rebuild of a Blitz site (?).

terrain.name: Hampstead Heath / Whitestone Pond summit
terrain.notes: Bagshot Sand capping Claygate Beds over London Clay; the highest point in inner London and the source of the Fleet, Tyburn and Westbourne.

terrain.name: Parliament Hill
terrain.notes: Classic protected sightline to St Paul's, 6.8 km away.

terrain.name: Primrose Hill
terrain.notes: Detached knoll south of the Heath ridge; protected view of the City.

terrain.name: Harrow on the Hill
terrain.notes: An outlier of Claygate Beds and Bagshot Sand rising abruptly out of the clay plain; visible from 20 km.

terrain.name: Shooter's Hill
terrain.notes: The highest point in south-east London; Blackheath Pebble Beds over London Clay. Severndroog Castle (1784) marks the summit.

terrain.name: Greenwich Park / One Tree Hill
terrain.notes: The Royal Observatory sits on the sharp Thanet Sand and gravel scarp above the river terrace.

terrain.name: Blackheath plateau
terrain.notes: Blackheath Beds gravel plateau; poor soil, hence common land.

terrain.name: Sydenham Hill / Crystal Palace
terrain.notes: The highest point in south London within the former LCC area; hence the Crystal Palace transmitter.

terrain.name: Honor Oak / One Tree Hill (Lewisham)
terrain.notes: Distinct from Greenwich Park's One Tree Hill. Fine northward view of the City.

terrain.name: Norwood ridge / Beulah Hill
terrain.notes: The Norwood ridge (the 'North Wood' of Croydon) is the watershed between the Effra and the Wandle catchments.

terrain.name: Addington Hills
terrain.notes: Blackheath Beds sand and gravel; one of the few heathland ridges in south London, with a famous view over central London.

terrain.name: Wimbledon Common / Putney Heath
terrain.notes: Gravel plateau of the Black Park/Boyn Hill terrace.

terrain.name: Richmond Hill / Richmond Park ridge
terrain.notes: King Henry's Mound, 55 m, has a legally protected sightline to St Paul's 16 km away (protected since 1710).

terrain.name: Ludgate Hill
terrain.notes: The western of the two gravel hills of Roman Londinium; St Paul's stands on its crest.

terrain.name: Cornhill
terrain.notes: The eastern hill of Londinium, site of the forum and basilica; the highest natural point in the City.

terrain.name: Barnet plateau / High Barnet
terrain.notes: Anglian glacial till plateau; the northern watershed of London, dividing the Brent and Lea catchments.

terrain.name: Hampstead Garden Suburb / Bishops Avenue ridge
Epping Forest ridge / High Beach
terrain.notes: Bagshot and Claygate Beds ridge between the Lea and Roding valleys.

terrain.name: Chislehurst and Bromley ridge
terrain.notes: Chalk downs capped by Blackheath Beds; the northern edge of the North Downs dip slope.

terrain.name: Biggin Hill / Westerham Heights
terrain.notes: Westerham Heights, 245 m, is the highest point in Greater London, on the North Downs escarpment.

terrain.name: Crystal Palace transmitter summit
terrain.notes: Duplicate of the Sydenham Hill blob at finer scale; use one or the other, not both (?).

terrain.name: Thames floodplain (Alluvium)
terrain.notes: Base level, not a blob: the tidal floodplain of alluvium and peat, 1-5 m AOD, covering Lambeth, Southwark, Bermondsey, the Isle of Dogs, the Lea mouth and the Erith levels. Use as the datum plane.

terrain.name: Taplow (Upper Floodplain) terrace
terrain.notes: Terrace level, not a blob: the low gravel terrace on which the City, Westminster, Chelsea and Fulham stand, typically 5-12 m AOD, a couple of metres above the marsh - the dry land that determined where London could be founded.

terrain.name: Boyn Hill / Lynch Hill terrace
terrain.notes: Terrace level: the higher gravel terraces at Ealing, Acton, Hounslow, Clapham and Wimbledon, roughly 20-35 m AOD.

terrain.name: London Clay plain
terrain.notes: Background level: the undulating London Clay country of north and outer London between the terraces and the Northern Heights, typically 30-60 m AOD.

forests_and_marshes.name: Forest of Middlesex (the Great Middlesex Forest)
forests_and_marshes.land_cover: oak, hornbeam and hazel wood pasture on London Clay
forests_and_marshes.notes: William FitzStephen described London in c.1174 as bordered on the north by 'a great forest, with wooded glades and lairs of wild animals, deer both red and fallow, wild boars and bulls'. Formally disafforested (removed from forest law) in 1218 by Henry III at the petition of the Londoners, after which clearance for arable and the London fuel and timber trade accelerated. Substantially cleared by 1400, though woods survived at Highgate, Enfield Chase (a royal chase until 1777), Hadley, Ruislip and Bishop's Wood. Boundary is a schematic envelope (?).

forests_and_marshes.name: Forest of Essex / Waltham Forest (Epping and Hainault)
forests_and_marshes.land_cover: beech, oak and hornbeam wood pasture with heath
forests_and_marshes.notes: The whole county of Essex was afforested under the Normans. Enclosure by lords of the manor nibbled at it from the 17th century and accelerated 1851-1871. Hainault Forest was disafforested and about 400 ha grubbed up within six weeks in 1851-52. Epping Forest was saved by the City of London Corporation's Chancery suit of 1874 and the Epping Forest Act 1878, and dedicated to the public in 1882. Modern Epping Forest is about 2476 ha of the original.

forests_and_marshes.name: Lambeth Marsh and St George's Fields
forests_and_marshes.land_cover: tidal reed marsh, osier beds and gravel eyots
forests_and_marshes.notes: Tidal on the spring tides until the medieval river wall; drained enough for market gardens and 'places of resort' by the 17th century but still semi-rural and flood-prone into the 1780s. Built over rapidly after Westminster (1750) and Blackfriars (1769) bridges and their approach roads.

forests_and_marshes.name: West Ham and Plaistow Levels
forests_and_marshes.land_cover: brackish grazing marsh with saltings
forests_and_marshes.notes: Grazing marsh embanked from the medieval period. Its cheapness and lack of building regulation drew the Royal Victoria Dock (1855), Beckton Gasworks (1870), the Thames Ironworks and the noxious trades expelled from the metropolis by the Metropolis Management Act 1855 - creating Silvertown, Canning Town and Beckton.

forests_and_marshes.name: Erith, Plumstead and Woolwich Marshes
forests_and_marshes.land_cover: brackish grazing marsh
forests_and_marshes.notes: The last large area of open marsh in London. Occupied by the Royal Arsenal ranges (from 1805), Crossness Sewage Works (1865), Thamesmead (from 1967) and, on the surviving fragment, Erith Marshes / Crossness Nature Reserve.

forests_and_marshes.name: Barking and Dagenham Levels
forests_and_marshes.land_cover: grazing marsh, saltings and fishing creeks
forests_and_marshes.notes: The river wall was breached in 1707, creating the Dagenham Breach lake, not fully repaired until 1721. Barking was England's largest fishing port in the 1850s. The levels became the Ford Dagenham plant (1931) and the Becontree Estate hinterland.

forests_and_marshes.name: Hackney and Walthamstow Marshes
forests_and_marshes.land_cover: freshwater Lammas grazing marsh with alder and willow carr
forests_and_marshes.notes: Lammas land: common grazing from Lammas Day (1 August) to Lady Day, held in severalty for hay in summer. Enclosure resisted through the 19th century; bought for the public 1893 (Hackney Marshes) and preserved 1905 (Walthamstow Marshes, the last semi-natural floodplain marsh in London). Hackney Marshes levelled with Blitz rubble from 1945; Walthamstow Marshes is an SSSI.

forests_and_marshes.name: Lea Valley marshes (Tottenham, Edmonton, Enfield, Waltham)
forests_and_marshes.land_cover: freshwater floodplain marsh, osier beds and reedbeds
forests_and_marshes.notes: Progressively taken for reservoirs (1852-1951), gunpowder and small-arms works (Waltham Abbey, Enfield Lock), sewage works and the glasshouse nurseries of the Lea Valley 'glasshouse industry' (from the 1880s). Designated the Lee Valley Regional Park in 1967 - Britain's first regional park.

forests_and_marshes.name: Stepney/Poplar Marsh (Isle of Dogs)
forests_and_marshes.land_cover: embanked grazing marsh
forests_and_marshes.notes: See water_history.json for the embanking, 1448 breach and re-drainage sequence. Effectively rural until the West India Docks (1802-1806).

forests_and_marshes.name: Battersea Fields and the Nine Elms marsh
forests_and_marshes.land_cover: damp riverside common and market gardens
forests_and_marshes.notes: Famous for its asparagus (Battersea Bundles), Sunday fairs and the Duke of Wellington's duel with Lord Winchilsea (1829). Enclosed 1846, raised with dock spoil and opened as Battersea Park in 1858.

forests_and_marshes.name: Hounslow Heath
forests_and_marshes.land_cover: acid heath and gravel commons
forests_and_marshes.notes: Once about 1600 ha of open heath on the Taplow gravels between Hounslow, Staines and Feltham. General Roy measured the Ordnance Survey's founding baseline across it in 1784. Enclosed under Acts from 1813-1818; the remainder went to barracks, gravel pits, the Great West Aerodrome (1929) and Heathrow Airport (requisitioned 1944). Only about 80 ha of heath remain.

forests_and_marshes.name: Finchley Common
forests_and_marshes.land_cover: scrubby clay heath and wood pasture
forests_and_marshes.notes: A remnant of the Forest of Middlesex on the Great North Road, second only to Hounslow Heath as highwayman country (Dick Turpin, Jack Sheppard). Enclosed by Act in 1816; almost nothing survives except fragments at Coldfall Wood and Finchley golf courses.

forests_and_marshes.name: Hampstead Heath
forests_and_marshes.land_cover: sandy heath, gorse and oak-birch wood on Bagshot Sand
forests_and_marshes.notes: Survives as heath because the sandy soil was worthless for arable and because the sand was dug for London's building trade. Protected 1871; extended to about 320 ha by later purchases.

forests_and_marshes.name: Wimbledon Common and Putney Heath
forests_and_marshes.land_cover: acid heath, gorse, birch and oak on gravel
forests_and_marshes.notes: About 460 ha protected by Act in 1871. Contains Caesar's Camp, an Iron Age univallate hillfort of c.500 BCE, and Wimbledon Windmill (1817).

forests_and_marshes.name: Blackheath
forests_and_marshes.land_cover: gravel heath
forests_and_marshes.notes: About 87 ha; pitted with old gravel and chalk workings. A muster and assembly ground for centuries - Wat Tyler 1381, Jack Cade 1450, the reception of Henry V after Agincourt 1415 and of Anne of Cleves 1540.

forests_and_marshes.name: Woolwich Common
forests_and_marshes.land_cover: acid grassland and heath
forests_and_marshes.notes: Bought by the Board of Ordnance in 1774 for the Royal Artillery; military use preserved it from building. About 63 ha; SINC for acid grassland.

forests_and_marshes.name: Enfield Chase
forests_and_marshes.land_cover: royal chase: oak and hornbeam wood pasture with lawns
forests_and_marshes.notes: About 3200 ha of royal hunting chase, part of the Forest of Middlesex, held by the Crown and the Duchy of Lancaster. Disafforested and divided by Act in 1777; the deer were dispersed and most of it enclosed and farmed by 1800. Trent Park, Hadley Wood and Whitewebbs are surviving fragments.

forests_and_marshes.name: Moorfields (the moor outside the City wall)
forests_and_marshes.land_cover: boggy fen fed by the Walbrook headwaters
forests_and_marshes.notes: Waterlogged ground immediately north of the wall, used for archery, bleaching linen and skating (FitzStephen describes Londoners skating on it on bone skates in the 1170s). First drained 1527, laid out with walks in 1606-1607 as one of London's earliest public gardens, and finally built over c.1777-1815; Finsbury Circus (1815) is its last open remnant. Bethlem Hospital moved here in 1676.

forests_and_marshes.name: Tothill Fields and Westminster marsh
forests_and_marshes.land_cover: wet meadow, osier beds and gravel eyots
forests_and_marshes.notes: Abbey land around Thorney Island: fairs, duels, a plague pit (1665) and the Tothill Fields Bridewell (1618-1884). Raised and built over as Pimlico and Victoria between about 1825 and 1855; Westminster Cathedral (1895-1903) stands on the prison site.

forests_and_marshes.name: St John's Wood and the Middlesex woods north-west of the city
forests_and_marshes.land_cover: oak and hornbeam wood, later pasture
forests_and_marshes.notes: Named for the Knights of St John of Jerusalem, who held it from the 12th century. Cleared for pasture by the 17th century and laid out from 1794-1820 as London's first suburb of detached and semi-detached villas rather than terraces - a template copied worldwide.
